Here is a parent-facing explanation you could use or adapt.

---

## Why the school is changing the way maths is taught

We know this is an important change, and we understand that some parents may be worried about it. We want to explain clearly why we are moving from **streaming by ability** to **mixed-attainment teaching** in mathematics.

### What is changing?

Until now, pupils have been placed into maths groups based on how they have performed in the past. This is often called **setting** or **streaming**.

From now on, we will teach maths in **mixed-attainment groups**. This means pupils with different starting points will learn together in the same class.

### Why are we making this change?

We are making this change because we want **every child to have the best chance to succeed in maths**.

Research and experience in many schools show that when children are grouped too early or too rigidly by “ability,” it can sometimes hold pupils back rather than help them.

### What can go wrong with streaming?

When children are placed in lower groups, they may:

- miss out on learning the same rich maths as others
- get less challenge
- start to believe they are “bad at maths”
- lose confidence and interest
- find it harder to move to higher work later on

When children are placed in higher groups, they can also be affected if the class moves too quickly and they do not get enough support when they need it.

### Why mixed-attainment teaching can help

In mixed-attainment classes, all pupils are still challenged, but in different ways. Teachers can support children and stretch them within the same lesson.

This approach can help pupils to:

- stay in the same class with a wider range of classmates
- hear different ways of solving problems
- build confidence
- take part in more discussion
- keep high expectations for everyone
- make strong progress over time

### Does this mean children will all do the same work?

No. It does **not** mean every child will do exactly the same task in the same way.

Teachers will still:

- give extra support where needed
- provide harder work for pupils who are ready for it
- check understanding carefully
- adapt lessons so children can succeed at different levels

The difference is that pupils will learn together in one class, rather than being separated into groups that may not change easily.

### Will children still make progress?

Yes. Our aim is for every child to make good progress. We will keep tracking how pupils are doing and will give extra help when it is needed.

We will also review how the system is working to make sure it is helping children learn well.

### Why now?

We want to make sure our maths teaching gives all pupils the best chance to:

- understand maths deeply
- become more confident
- enjoy learning maths
- achieve well in the long term

We believe this change will help us do that.

### We understand parents may have questions

Many parents want the best for their children and may feel unsure about this change. That is completely understandable.

If you were taught in a system where children were separated by “ability,” it can feel strange to do things differently. But teaching has changed because we know more now about how children learn best.

We would be happy to talk with you if you have concerns or would like to know more.

### In short

We are changing because we believe mixed-attainment teaching will:

- help more children succeed
- keep expectations high for everyone
- build confidence in maths
- avoid limiting children too early

Our goal is simple: **to help every child do as well as they can in maths**.
